title: Dollars per child, over time
question: How did City and State early-childhood money move against the number of young children living in the city and the number of licensed places?
finding: City early-childhood payments went from $117.7 million in fiscal 2019 to $297.3 million in fiscal 2026 while children under five fell from 36,864 to 32,320: $3,192 per child then, $9,198 now. State contracts to San Francisco agencies add $219.6 million in 2025-26, making $15,993 per child under five, or $20,732 for each of the 24,933 centre places with a licence in force in July 2025 (23,800 in July 2020). 83% of the City money in fiscal 2026 went to three pass-through agencies. In fiscal 2025 the City counted 9,150 children receiving funded care, $20,690 each ($24,922 if payments are counted in the year the City's file labels them); the City's published full-time preschool rate is $25,380 a year. In 2010 the budget analyst put the whole City early-care budget at $66.2 million.
how: City money is every payment in the voucher table by the Department of Early Childhood and the Children and Families Commission, plus Human Services Agency payments under early-care contracts (found by contract title) before the department was created in fiscal 2023; each payment is counted in the fiscal year its voucher number belongs to. State money is the sum of contract maximums for San Francisco agencies other than City departments (published from 2022-23); contracts the State gives to City departments are shown separately because the City pays them on. Children under five are Census Bureau estimates for 1 July at the start of each fiscal year; children under six are State Department of Finance figures. State preschool figures are on file from 2023-24, so State money is shown from fiscal 2024. Centre places are the capacity of every licence in force on 1 July of each year, rebuilt from the State licensing file (possible from 2020, when the file's record of closed licences begins; licences since marked inactive are included); the rebuilt figure for 1 July 2023 is 25,124 and the State's own count two days earlier was 24,702. Children receiving funded care is the City's own performance measure.
limits: Dollars per child under five divides by every young child in the city (the City counted 29% of them as receiving funded care in fiscal 2025), so it measures the size of the effort, not what a child's care costs. The rise follows the commercial rents tax for early care and education (Proposition C), whose spending plan is dated August 2019: a decision of policy, not an anomaly. State figures are maximums, not payments. City payments include buildings, wage supplements for teachers and family resource centres, not only care. Some Human Services Agency early-care payments with untypical contract titles will be missed before fiscal 2023. The two population sources disagree (for July 2024 the State counts 37,095 children under five and the Census Bureau 32,028), and the State's figures after 2024 are projections. Fiscal 2027 is in progress ($165.1 million so far) and is left off. The payment file labels each line with a fiscal year that is not always the year the payment was issued: some earlier payments, mostly on purchase orders in multi-year capital funds, are filed under a later year, and the Controller's own published figures follow that label. Payments are dated here by voucher number, a single running sequence, which moves $5.52 billion of $119.3 billion (4.6%) to an earlier year than its label; $1.08 billion of that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier, before the file starts. Near the turn of a year the number dates a payment to within a few days. $1.5 million of these payments carries a number from fiscal 2018 or earlier and is in no year's figure.
